title: Investigating Quantum-Embedded Transformers on Classical Datasets for Cross-Modality Classification
abstract: We test whether a parameterized quantum circuit (PQC) improves a hybrid quantum-classical model's performance on classical datasets, using an interface-matched classical map as the control while holding all other components fixed. Our architecture, Quantum-Embedded Attention (QEA), uses a learnable projector to compress backbone features into an $n_q$-dimensional angle vector, a shallow PQC to map those angles to one- and two-qubit Pauli expectations, and a classical attention decoder to produce class logits. We hypothesized the PQC would improve accuracy or seed-to-seed stability over a classical map with matched input/output dimensions. We test this with an interface-matched $2\times2$ factorial on Breast Cancer Wisconsin at $n_q\in\{4,8\}$, independently swapping the PQC for a classical map and the attention decoder for a linear head, across five paired seeds per cell. Three of four paired quantum-minus-classical $95\%$ confidence intervals include zero; the fourth, a $+1.63$ percentage-point contrast for the attention decoder at $n_q=4$, reverses sign at $n_q=8$ and does not survive correction across the four contrasts. The experiment thus shows no consistent PQC contribution and cannot establish equivalence. A five-dataset cross-modality grid shows comparable accuracy on AG~News, Breast Cancer Wisconsin, and BirdCLEF but a large deficit on CIFAR-10; these cells are not interface-matched and are interpreted descriptively. We report all planned canonical runs, distinguish current Pauli-readout results from legacy probability-readout experiments, and analyze bottleneck, simulation, finite-shot, and noise limitations. The results do not establish a quantum advantage; they demonstrate why controlled component attribution is necessary before crediting a hybrid model's performance to its quantum layer.
summary: This work tests a hybrid transformer model incorporating a Parameterized Quantum Circuit (PQC) for cross-modality classification. By performing controlled component attribution studies against classical baselines, the authors found no consistent evidence of a quantum advantage from the PQC layer. The study emphasizes that careful methodological controls are necessary before any performance gains can be attributed to the quantum components.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether integrating a Parameterized Quantum Circuit (PQC) into a hybrid quantum-classical transformer architecture improves performance on classical cross-modality classification tasks.
main_result: The controlled factorial analysis failed to show any consistent or statistically significant contribution from the PQC, concluding that no quantum advantage was established under the tested protocol.
method: A rigorous component attribution study using an interface-matched $2 	imes 2$ factorial design was employed, systematically replacing the PQC with classical maps and the attention decoder with linear heads.
model_or_system: The model is Quantum-Embedded Attention (QEA), which processes features through a learnable projector into an angle vector ($\xi$), feeds this into a shallow PQC acting on qubits to generate Pauli expectation values ($\mathbf{m}$), and finally uses a classical attention decoder.
key_observables: Paired performance differences ($\Delta Q-C$) derived from the factorial analysis, accuracy metrics across multiple datasets (e.g., Breast Cancer Wisconsin).
important_parameters: $n_q$ (number of qubits), $2 	imes 2$ factorial structure, and controlled comparison against classical baselines.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that component contributions can be isolated via interface-matched controls; the results are limited to ideal statevector simulations without hardware noise modeling.
figures_summary: Notes reference tables detailing forward costs (scaling with $n_q$) and parameter counts for the factorial analysis, but no specific figure summaries were extracted.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the QEA architecture, details the controlled component attribution methodology using a factorial design, presents results showing non-significant quantum contributions, discusses cross-modality performance descriptively, and concludes by emphasizing methodological rigor over claiming advantage.
why_interesting: While focused on ML classification, the rigorous testing of PQC components against classical counterparts provides valuable insights into the necessary conditions for demonstrating genuine quantum utility in hybrid models, which is relevant to understanding resource scaling in complex quantum simulations.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: The core QEA pipeline of Eq. (2). A classical backbone and projector reduce the input to an nq-dimensional angle vector, a parameterized quantum circuit produces a vector of measurement statistics, and an attention decoder maps those statistics to class logits. The two dashed switches define the interface-matched factorial of Section 4: switch A replaces the circuit with an equal- width classical map, and switch B replaces the attention decoder with a linear head. The broader exploratory grid uses the QEA-R variant, which additionally concatenates the projected angles as a residual token stream; that variant is reported separately and is not used for component attribution.

Figure 2: Paired quantum-minus-classical switch-A effects in the BCW factorial. Points denote the mean within-seed difference and error bars the 95% Student-t interval over five paired seeds. The vertical line marks zero. The plot makes visible both the isolated positive nq = 4 attention contrast and its failure to replicate at nq = 8; numerical values are in Table 2.

Figure 3: Exploratory cross-dataset comparison corresponding to Table 4. Error bars are 95% Student-t intervals; fill patterns distinguish methods without relying on color. The figure shows similar point estimates on three datasets, a QEA-R deficit on SUSY, and a large failure of both quantum models on CIFAR-10.
